title: StarGuard is the preferred execution method because it moves Agent Spell execution out of the Sky Core transaction
content:
A.1.10.2.3.2.3 offers two ways to execute an Agent Spell and states a preference: "Execution through StarGuard is the preferred method and any exceptions require valid reasoning."

The alternative shows what is being avoided. Under direct execution (A.1.10.2.3.2.3.2.1) the Sky Core Spell "directly calls `exec()` on the Agent's SubProxy contract to perform the Spell's actions **in the same transaction**." Every Agent's logic then shares the Core Spell's atomicity and gas budget: one Agent's revert or gas exhaustion is the Core Spell's failure.

StarGuard breaks that coupling. Per A.1.10.2.3.2.3.1, "the Sky Core Spell includes a whitelist of approved Agent Spells, which allows them to be executed via separate transactions," which "enhances resilience and scalability, ensuring robust handling of payloads from multiple active Agents while minimizing risks to Sky Core." A.1.10.2.3.2.3.1.1.2 adds that whitelisting "allows Agent Spells to run independently, supporting arbitrary complexity and custom features like office hours or expiration times."

The governance consequence is the interesting part: Sky Core's vote commits to a *codehash*, not to an execution. Approval and execution become separable events, which is what makes A.1.10.2.3.2.3.1.1.2's `drop()` function possible — "a mechanism to revoke access if needed for security or error correction" after the vote has already passed. Direct execution has no such window; the vote and the effect are the same atomic act.

Ownership keeps the arrangement from widening authority: the StarGuard contract is owned by the Pause Proxy (A.1.10.2.3.2.3.1.1.2.1) and "only the owner, the Pause Proxy, is able to whitelist new Agent Spells via a Sky Core Spell" (A.1.10.2.3.2.3.1.1.2.3). Execution is decoupled; authorization is not.
description: Sky Core only whitelists a codehash; the Agent Spell then runs in its own transaction, so arbitrary Agent complexity cannot endanger the Core Spell — and drop() can revoke approval before execution.
